How Weather and Dome vs. Outdoor Venues Move NFL Totals

Published August 23, 2026 · 10 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Ask a handful of bettors why a Sunday total opened at 41 instead of 45 and most will eventually mention weather. That instinct is correct, but it's usually applied too bluntly — "wind is bad for scoring" is true on average and nearly useless in practice, because the size of the effect depends heavily on which stadium the game is in, what kind of roof it has, and what specific weather variable is actually in play. A 12 mph crosswind at a stadium with a low, tight bowl does something very different to passing offense than the same wind reading at an open, elevated venue.

Three venue types, not two

Most bettors sort NFL venues into "dome" and "outdoor," but for total-setting purposes there are really three relevant categories: fixed domes (Ford Field, Mercedes-Benz Stadium, Caesars Superdome, U.S. Bank Stadium, State Farm Stadium with its roof typically closed), retractable-roof stadiums that play some games open and some closed (AT&T Stadium, Allegiant Stadium, SoFi Stadium's roofless-but-covered design, Lucas Oil Stadium), and fully open-air outdoor stadiums with no roof option at all (Lambeau Field, Highmark Stadium, Soldier Field, Arrowhead Stadium, and most of the rest of the league). The first category removes weather from the total-setting equation almost entirely. The second category means the market has to price in real uncertainty about roof status until it's confirmed, sometimes as late as pregame warmups. The third category is where the bulk of weather-driven total movement in the NFL actually happens.

This distinction matters because "outdoor stadium in October" isn't a single condition — a 60-degree, calm evening at Lambeau and a 25 mph gusting crosswind at the same stadium in December are both "outdoor games," but only one of them is a total-moving weather event.

Why wind matters more than cold, and why direction matters more than speed

Temperature alone has a surprisingly small, inconsistent effect on scoring once you control for wind — cold hands and a harder football matter at the margins, but plenty of low-scoring cold-weather games turn out to be low-scoring mostly because they're also windy games, and plenty of frigid, calm games play a normal total. Wind is the variable with the clearest, most repeatable relationship to scoring, because it directly degrades the accuracy of the passing game, which is where most modern NFL scoring comes from. A sustained wind in the mid-teens (mph) or higher is generally treated by bettors and total-setters as meaningful; anything under about 10 mph is largely noise.

Direction and consistency matter as much as raw speed. A steady crosswind that holds through the game is more disruptive to a passing offense than a stronger but gusting, inconsistent wind, because quarterbacks and kickers can partially adjust to a predictable crosswind but can't reliably adjust to wind that changes by 10 mph and shifts direction snap to snap. Stadium geometry compounds this: a bowl-shaped, enclosed-sideline stadium like Lambeau can actually swirl wind unpredictably at field level even when the forecast reading from a nearby weather station looks moderate, while a more open venue tends to produce steadier, more predictable wind that's easier for both teams — and the market — to price.

Rain and snow: a different mechanism than wind

Precipitation affects scoring through a different channel than wind — it's less about accuracy in the air and more about ball security and footing. Heavy, sustained rain tends to push a game toward more rushing attempts and fewer possessions overall as both teams try to shorten the game and avoid fumbles, which can lower scoring somewhat, but the effect is generally smaller and less consistent than a strong, steady wind. Snow is more variable still: a light, steady snow with good field conditions underneath often has a minimal effect on scoring, while heavy, wet, accumulating snow that affects both footing and visibility is a bigger factor. The practical takeaway is that "rain" or "snow" in a forecast is a much weaker total-moving signal on its own than "15+ mph sustained wind," and treating all precipitation forecasts as equally significant is a common bettor mistake.

A worked example: the same total, two forecasts

Take a hypothetical outdoor AFC North matchup that would open around 44 in perfectly calm conditions, based purely on the two offenses and defenses involved. If the forecast settles into a mild, dry, 8 mph breeze, that total likely stays close to 44 all week — normal weather noise, nothing for the market to specifically price. Now change only the wind forecast to a steady 20 mph gusting to 30, still with the same two teams and the same dry conditions. That specific forecast, on its own, is often enough to pull a total down two to three points by kickoff as sportsbooks and sharp bettors both react to the passing-game impact, even though nothing about the teams' actual talent changed. The gap between those two scenarios is the entire point of this guide: weather isn't a total modifier bettors apply uniformly, it's a specific, variable-by-variable adjustment that mostly comes down to wind speed and consistency at outdoor stadiums.

Takeaway: If you're evaluating a total at an outdoor stadium, check the wind forecast specifically — not just the general weather icon — and weight steady wind in the mid-teens or higher far more heavily than temperature or a generic rain/snow forecast.

Retractable roofs and the closed-roof wrinkle

Retractable-roof stadiums add a layer sharp bettors track that casual bettors often miss entirely: roof status isn't always locked in when a total first opens, and it can shift market pricing once it's confirmed. Some franchises have historically closed the roof more often than league-average regardless of forecast, which effectively neutralizes weather as a total-moving factor for that game no matter what the outside conditions look like. Others play more games open than their opponents might expect. Because roof decisions are sometimes announced only a day or two out — or later — totals at these venues can carry real uncertainty right up until that news breaks, and a total that looked "weather-exposed" on Tuesday can look completely different by Saturday once the roof call is public.

How and when this actually shows up in the line

Weather forecasts firm up considerably in the final 72 hours before an NFL game, and that's usually when you'll see totals start moving specifically in response to wind or precipitation updates rather than team-news factors. A total that opened Tuesday based on team quality alone can shift meaningfully by Friday or Saturday purely because a forecast update changed the expected wind speed at kickoff, with no new information about either roster. This is also where line shopping matters most for weather-driven totals specifically — not every sportsbook updates its number at the same speed or by the same amount when a forecast changes, so the same game can carry a real total gap between operators in the final day or two before kickoff. For the broader mechanics of how totals get set and moved in the first place, see our NFL betting guide.

Common mistakes bettors make with weather totals

The most frequent error is reacting to the weather icon rather than the actual numbers — a "rain" forecast reads as scarier than a calm 8 mph breeze, even though the wind reading is the variable that matters more in most cases. A close second is ignoring venue type entirely and assuming every outdoor stadium in a cold-weather city behaves identically; stadium geometry genuinely changes how a given wind reading translates to on-field disruption. A third is betting a weather angle too early, before the forecast has firmed up — a Tuesday forecast for a Sunday game carries real uncertainty, and totals that already moved on early, shaky forecast data sometimes correct back the other way once a more reliable short-range forecast lands. Finally, remember that weather affects both teams' offenses, not just one — the practical betting angle is almost always about the total, not automatically about which team benefits, since a bad-weather game usually suppresses both sides roughly proportionally rather than favoring the run-heavier team outright in every case.

Frequently asked questions

How much wind does it actually take to move an NFL total?

Sustained wind below roughly 10 mph is generally treated as noise. The range where bettors and total-setters start reacting meaningfully is typically in the mid-teens and up, with steady wind in the 20+ mph range associated with more significant total adjustments.

Does cold weather by itself lower scoring?

The standalone effect of cold temperature, without wind, is small and inconsistent. Most of what looks like a "cold weather" scoring effect in casual analysis is actually a wind effect, since cold outdoor games in December and January are also frequently windy games.

Why do retractable-roof games sometimes still get weather-adjusted totals?

Because roof status isn't always confirmed when a total is first posted. Until the roof decision is public, the market has to account for the possibility the game is played open, and totals can shift once that uncertainty is resolved either way.

Is rain or snow a bigger factor than wind?

Generally no. Precipitation tends to have a smaller, less consistent effect on scoring than a strong, steady wind, mainly influencing game script (more rushing, fewer possessions) rather than directly degrading passing accuracy the way wind does.

When should I actually look at the weather forecast for betting purposes?

Forecasts become meaningfully more reliable inside the final 72 hours before kickoff. Reacting to a weather angle much earlier than that means reacting to forecast data that's still likely to change.
